questions.q: Which element is in the p block of the Periodic Table?
questions.solution: Gallium (\(\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^{10}\,4s^{2}\,4p^{1}}\)) has its highest-energy electron in a p sub-shell, so it is in the p block. Potassium and strontium are s block. (Zinc is a common wrong choice: its last electron enters the 3d sub-shell, so it is d block.)

questions.q: Which statement explains the trend in atomic radius from sodium to chlorine?

options.A: The radius decreases because the nuclear charge increases while the shielding stays about the same.
options.B: The radius increases because each element has more electrons.
options.C: The radius decreases because the shielding increases.
options.D: The radius decreases because each element has an extra electron shell.

questions.solution: Across Period 3 the electrons are added to the same shell, so shielding hardly changes, while the number of protons rises. The outer electrons are pulled closer to the nucleus. (Thinking more electrons make atoms bigger across a period is the common slip.)

questions.q: Why is the first ionisation energy of aluminium lower than that of magnesium?

options.A: The electron removed from aluminium is in a 3p orbital that already holds another electron, so the pair repels.
options.B: Aluminium has a smaller nuclear charge than magnesium.
options.C: The electron removed from aluminium is in a 3p sub-shell, higher in energy than the 3s electron removed from magnesium.
options.D: The outer electron of aluminium is in a new, more shielded shell.

questions.solution: Magnesium loses a 3s electron; aluminium loses a 3p electron, which is higher in energy and slightly shielded by the 3s electrons, so less energy is needed. (Electron-pair repulsion explains the drop at sulfur, not at aluminium.)

questions.q: Four consecutive elements in Period 3, W, X, Y and Z, have first ionisation energies of 1012, 1000, 1251 and 1521 \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). Which element is X?
questions.solution: The only fall in first ionisation energy after silicon in Period 3 is from phosphorus to sulfur, where a paired 3p electron is removed. So W is phosphorus, X is sulfur, Y chlorine and Z argon. (Taking the dip to be at aluminium is the common slip; the energies are far too high for that.)

questions.q: Which element in Period 3 has the highest melting point?
questions.solution: Silicon has a giant covalent structure: melting it means breaking many strong covalent bonds. The metals have metallic bonding and phosphorus is simple molecular. (Aluminium is often chosen because its metallic bonding is the strongest of the three metals, but it melts far lower than silicon.)

questions.q: Why does sulfur have a higher melting point than phosphorus?

options.A: \(\mathrm{S_{8}}\) molecules have more electrons than \(\mathrm{P_{4}}\) molecules, so the van der Waals forces between them are stronger.
options.B: The S–S covalent bonds are stronger than the P–P covalent bonds.
options.C: Sulfur has more delocalised electrons than phosphorus.
options.D: \(\mathrm{S_{8}}\) molecules are polar, but \(\mathrm{P_{4}}\) molecules are not.

questions.solution: Both are simple molecular, so melting overcomes only the forces between molecules. \(\mathrm{S_{8}}\) (128 electrons) has more electrons than \(\mathrm{P_{4}}\) (60), so its van der Waals forces are stronger. (Breaking covalent bonds on melting is the common slip.)

questions.q: Why do the melting points increase from sodium to magnesium to aluminium?

options.A: The atoms get heavier, so more energy is needed to separate them.
options.B: The van der Waals forces between the atoms get stronger.
options.C: The metal ions are smaller and more highly charged, and there are more delocalised electrons, so the metallic bonding is stronger.
options.D: The covalent character of the bonding increases.

questions.solution: Na, Mg and Al give 1, 2 and 3 delocalised electrons per atom, forming \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\), \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\), which are also smaller. The attraction between the ions and the sea of electrons increases. (Explaining it by mass is the common slip.)

questions.q: Silicon has the highest melting point in Period 3. Which element shows the same feature in Period 2?
questions.solution: Carbon is in the same group as silicon and also forms a giant covalent structure (diamond or graphite), so it has the highest melting point in Period 2. The repeating pattern across periods is periodicity. (Choosing boron, which is also giant covalent but melts lower, is the common slip.)

questions.q: A graph of first ionisation energy against atomic number for elements 1 to 20 shows a repeating pattern. Where are the peaks?
questions.solution: Each period ends with a noble gas, which has the greatest nuclear charge for its shell and a full outer shell, so its first ionisation energy is the highest in the period. The minimum follows straight after, at the Group 1 metal. (Mixing up the peaks and the troughs is the common slip.)

questions.q: Which equation shows the reaction of magnesium with steam?
questions.solution: Hot magnesium burns in steam to give magnesium oxide and hydrogen. With cold water the reaction is very slow and gives magnesium hydroxide; at the high temperature of the steam reaction, the oxide forms instead. (Writing magnesium hydroxide as the product with steam is the common slip.)

questions.q: Which oxide gives a solution of about pH 13 when added to water?
questions.solution: Sodium oxide is ionic; its oxide ions react with water to give a concentrated solution of sodium hydroxide: \(\mathrm{Na_{2}O + H_{2}O \rightarrow 2NaOH}\), pH about 13. Magnesium oxide is only slightly soluble (pH about 9), aluminium oxide is insoluble (pH 7), and sulfur dioxide gives an acidic solution. (Choosing MgO overlooks its low solubility.)

questions.q: Which oxide reacts with both hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution?
questions.solution: Aluminium oxide is amphoteric: it reacts as a base with acids (forming \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\)) and as an acid with bases (forming \(\mathrm{[Al(OH)_{4}]^{-}}\)). Silicon dioxide reacts only with bases, magnesium oxide only with acids. (Silicon dioxide is often chosen because it is insoluble too, but it is acidic, not amphoteric.)

questions.q: Which equation shows the reaction of phosphorus(V) oxide with excess sodium hydroxide solution?
questions.solution: Acidic \(\mathrm{P_{4}O_{10}}\) is neutralised by excess hydroxide to sodium phosphate and water: \(\mathrm{P_{4}O_{10} + 12NaOH \rightarrow 4Na_{3}PO_{4} + 6H_{2}O}\). Check: 4 P, 12 Na, 12 H and 22 O on each side. The second equation leaves out two phosphorus atoms; the last is the reaction with water, not with sodium hydroxide. (Not balancing the water is the common slip.)

questions.q: Why does silicon dioxide have a much higher melting point than phosphorus(V) oxide, \(\mathrm{P_{4}O_{10}}\)?

options.A: The covalent bonds inside \(\mathrm{P_{4}O_{10}}\) molecules are weaker than those in \(\mathrm{SiO_{2}}\).
options.C: \(\mathrm{SiO_{2}}\) has hydrogen bonds between its molecules.
options.D: \(\mathrm{SiO_{2}}\) is giant covalent, so strong covalent bonds must break; \(\mathrm{P_{4}O_{10}}\) is simple molecular, so only weak forces between molecules must be overcome.

questions.solution: Melting \(\mathrm{SiO_{2}}\) breaks its giant covalent network. \(\mathrm{P_{4}O_{10}}\) molecules stay intact when it melts; only van der Waals forces and dipole–dipole forces are overcome. (Comparing the strength of covalent bonds inside the molecules is the common slip.)

questions.q: Which species forms when sulfur dioxide dissolves in water?
questions.solution: \(\mathrm{SO_{2} + H_{2}O \rightarrow H_{2}SO_{3}}\): sulfuric(IV) acid (sulfurous acid), which partly dissociates to \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) and \(\mathrm{HSO_{3}^{-}}\). Sulfur stays at +4. (Sulfuric(VI) acid, \(\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}}\), comes from \(\mathrm{SO_{3}}\), which is the common slip.)

questions.q: Which statement best describes the trend in the oxides from \(\mathrm{Na_{2}O}\) to \(\mathrm{SO_{3}}\)?

options.A: The bonding changes from covalent to ionic, and the oxides change from acidic to basic.
options.B: The bonding changes from ionic to covalent, and the oxides change from basic, through amphoteric, to acidic.
options.C: The bonding changes from ionic to covalent, and the oxides change from acidic to basic.
options.D: All the oxides are ionic, and they become more basic across the period.

questions.solution: Na, Mg and Al form giant ionic oxides; Si a giant covalent oxide; P and S simple molecular oxides. Ionic oxides contain \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\), which acts as a base, while the covalent oxides react with water to give acids, with \(\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}}\) amphoteric in between. (Reversing the acid–base trend is the common slip.)
